body:
Understanding pilgrimage

A pilgrimage is a journey undertaken to a place regarded as sacred or spiritually significant. Pilgrims may travel to worship, fulfil religious obligations, seek spiritual merit, express gratitude or participate in religious ceremonies.

In India, pilgrimage has historically connected people belonging to different regions, languages and social backgrounds. Pilgrimage routes have also encouraged the movement of religious ideas, literature, artistic traditions, merchants and artisans.

Sacred geography

Sacred geography refers to the association of geographical features and places with religious beliefs, sacred narratives, spiritual personalities and ritual practices. A mountain, river, forest, settlement or coastline may acquire religious significance through these associations.

Geographical featureExamples
Sacred riversGanga, Narmada, Godavari
Sacred mountainsGirnar, Shatrunjaya, Pavagadh
River confluencesTriveni Sangam at Prayagraj
Coastal pilgrimage centresDwarka, Somnath, Rameswaram
Sacred settlementsVaranasi, Mathura, Bodh Gaya

A cultural landscape develops through the interaction of people with their natural surroundings over time. Sacred landscapes are cultural landscapes in which religious meanings and practices are closely connected with geographical features.

Girnar illustrates this relationship. The mountain itself is sacred, while its temples, pathways, religious ceremonies and traditional circumambulation collectively form a living sacred landscape.

Important pilgrimage terms

  • Tirtha: A sacred place associated with spiritual merit, religious observance or liberation. The Sanskrit term originally conveys the idea of a crossing place.
  • Yatra: A religious journey or pilgrimage.
  • Dham: A sacred abode or important religious destination.
  • Parikrama or Pradakshina: Circumambulation of a sacred object, shrine, mountain, settlement or other sacred geographical feature.
  • Sangam: The confluence of rivers, which may possess religious significance.

Pilgrimage and religious tourism

Pilgrimage is primarily motivated by religious or spiritual purposes. Religious tourism includes travel to religious destinations for worship, historical interest, architecture, education or cultural experience.

The two categories overlap. A person visiting Somnath may be both a pilgrim and a tourist. Another visitor may visit the same temple primarily to understand its architectural and historical significance.

Sacred geography explains why a place is religiously significant. A pilgrimage network explains how people travel between and interact with such places.

Prelims focus

  • Sacred geography connects religious meaning with geographical places.
  • Parikrama and Pradakshina denote circumambulation.
  • Girnar, Shatrunjaya and Pavagadh are sacred hill landscapes in Gujarat.
  • Dwarka and Somnath are coastal pilgrimage centres.
  • Trap: Pilgrimage and tourism are overlapping, not mutually exclusive, categories.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts – I, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 10, pp. 105–106; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, pp. 49–50; Gujarat Tourism, Religious Sites and Girnar Hill, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Sacred Geography and the Meaning of Pilgrimage

body:
The formation of pilgrimage networks

A pilgrimage network consists of religious destinations connected through customary journeys, shared beliefs, festivals and transport routes. Networks may extend across India, remain within a particular region or follow a natural feature such as a river.

Indian pilgrimage networks have developed over centuries through religious texts, oral traditions, devotional movements, patronage and the repeated journeys of pilgrims.

Char Dham

The traditional all-India Char Dham consists of 4 major pilgrimage destinations situated in different geographical regions. The network is traditionally associated with Adi Shankaracharya.

DhamStateDirection
BadrinathUttarakhandNorth
DwarkaGujaratWest
Jagannath PuriOdishaEast
RameswaramTamil NaduSouth

These destinations are distinct from the Chota Char Dham of Uttarakhand, which consists of Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath.

Jyotirlinga network

The 12 Jyotirlingas are traditionally recognised sacred manifestations of Shiva. Their geographical distribution connects several regions of India through a common Shaiva pilgrimage tradition.

Gujarat has 2 commonly recognised Jyotirlinga destinations: Somnath and Nageshwar near Dwarka. Religious traditions differ regarding the identification of certain Jyotirlinga locations, so local claims should not always be treated as universally accepted geographical identifications.

Shakti Peethas

Shakti Peethas are sacred places associated with the worship of the divine feminine, particularly the traditions connected with Sati and Shakti. Their number and identification vary among religious texts and traditions. A widely followed enumeration recognises 51 Shakti Peethas.

Ambaji and Kalika Mata at Pavagadh are important Shakti pilgrimage centres in Gujarat.

Sapta Puri

The Sapta Puri tradition recognises 7 sacred cities associated with spiritual liberation. They are Ayodhya, Mathura, Haridwar, Kashi or Varanasi, Kanchipuram, Avantika or Ujjain, and Dwarka.

Dwarka therefore belongs to both the Char Dham and Sapta Puri traditions.

River and mountain pilgrimages

Not all pilgrimage networks consist of separate temples. Some journeys follow or encircle sacred natural features.

  • Narmada Parikrama: A customary pilgrimage along both banks of the Narmada, completing a circuit of the sacred river.
  • Girnar Lili Parikrama: A traditional circumambulation of the Girnar sacred landscape near Junagadh.
  • Shatrunjaya pilgrimage: A major Jain pilgrimage associated with Shatrunjaya Hill near Palitana.

Prelims focus

  • Traditional Char Dham: Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameswaram.
  • Chota Char Dham is located entirely in Uttarakhand.
  • Somnath and Nageshwar are Gujarat's commonly recognised Jyotirlinga destinations.
  • Dwarka is associated with both Char Dham and Sapta Puri.
  • Shakti Peethas are associated with goddess worship.
  • Trap: The 4 traditional all-India Dhams are not identical to the Chota Char Dham.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, pp. 49–50; Gujarat Tourism, Religious Sites and Krishna Circuit; Banaskantha District Administration, Ambaji Temple, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Traditional Char Dham spans north, west, east and south India; Chota Char Dham lies entirely in Uttarakhand, with Badrinath common to both.
pictures.caption: Traditional Char Dham and Chota Char Dham.

title: Major Hindu Pilgrimage Networks of India

body:
Buddhist pilgrimage

Buddhist pilgrimage is closely associated with places connected to the life, teachings and spiritual attainment of Gautama Buddha. These places became centres of worship, learning and monastic activity.

PlaceLocationAssociation
LumbiniNepalBirth of Buddha
Bodh GayaBiharAttainment of enlightenment
SarnathUttar PradeshFirst sermon
KushinagarUttar PradeshMahaparinirvana

Other important Buddhist destinations include Rajgir, Nalanda, Shravasti and Vaishali. Nalanda was an important centre of Buddhist monastic education.

Historical Buddhist pilgrimage

Chinese Buddhist pilgrims travelled to the Indian subcontinent to visit sacred places, study religious teachings and collect manuscripts.

  • Fa Xian: Visited India in the early 5th century CE.
  • Xuan Zang: Visited India in the 7th century CE and studied at Nalanda.
  • Yijing: Visited the Indian subcontinent in the late 7th century CE and contributed to the transmission of Buddhist learning.

Their journeys demonstrate that pilgrimage networks facilitated international cultural and intellectual exchange. Buddhist pilgrims frequently used the same land and maritime routes as merchants.

Jain pilgrimage

Jain sacred places are frequently associated with the lives, teachings and liberation of Tirthankaras. A Tirthankara is a spiritual teacher who shows the path towards liberation.

  • Palitana: Shatrunjaya Hill in Gujarat, associated particularly with Adinath or Rishabhanatha, the 1st Tirthankara.
  • Girnar: Gujarat, associated with Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara.
  • Sammed Shikharji: Parasnath Hill in Jharkhand, a major Jain pilgrimage destination.
  • Shatrunjaya and Girnar: Examples of sacred hill landscapes where the physical journey forms an important part of pilgrimage.

Sikh pilgrimage

Important Sikh religious destinations are associated with the Sikh Gurus and the history of the Sikh community.

Harmandir Sahib, popularly known as the Golden Temple, is located in Amritsar, Punjab. Sikh religious institutions are also associated with congregational worship, community service and the tradition of langar, a community kitchen serving meals without discrimination.

Kartarpur Sahib in present-day Pakistan is associated with Guru Nanak's later life. Sikh pilgrimage therefore also has an international geographical dimension.

Islamic and Sufi pilgrimage

The Hajj is the Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca in Saudi Arabia. It is a religious obligation for Muslims who possess the required physical and financial ability.

Within South Asia, visits to the tombs of Sufi saints constitute another important religious tradition. A dargah is the shrine or tomb of a revered religious figure, commonly a Sufi saint.

Ajmer Sharif in Rajasthan is associated with Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti. His shrine has historically attracted visitors from different religious communities. A khanqah, by contrast, is a Sufi religious establishment used for spiritual instruction, gatherings and hospitality.

Christian and Zoroastrian pilgrimage

Velankanni in Tamil Nadu is an important Christian pilgrimage centre associated with the Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health. Goa's churches also attract visitors interested in Christian religious traditions and architectural heritage.

Udvada in Gujarat's Valsad district is a major Zoroastrian religious destination. It is associated with the Iranshah Atash Bahram fire temple, which possesses great religious significance for the Parsi community.

Prelims focus

  • Lumbini: birth; Bodh Gaya: enlightenment; Sarnath: first sermon; Kushinagar: Mahaparinirvana.
  • Palitana is associated with the 1st Jain Tirthankara, Adinath.
  • Girnar is associated with the 22nd Jain Tirthankara, Neminatha.
  • Ajmer Sharif is associated with Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti.
  • Udvada is an important Zoroastrian religious centre.
  • Trap: Lumbini is in Nepal, not India.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts – I, 2018–19 edition, Chapters 7 and 10, pp. 105–106 for Buddhist travellers; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts – II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 8, pp. 111–118; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Buddhist Circuit Tourist Train; Gujarat Tourism, Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill, Girnar Hill and Udvada Parsi Fire Temple, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Four principal Buddhist pilgrimage destinations.

title: Buddhist, Jain, Sikh and Other Pilgrimage Traditions

body:
Historical development of temple towns

In ancient and medieval India, important religious establishments frequently became centres of settlement, employment, trade and cultural activity.

Rulers, merchants and devotees donated money, land, buildings and valuable objects to temples. Land grants could provide agricultural produce or revenue to maintain religious establishments, support their personnel, feed pilgrims and conduct festivals.

The regular arrival of pilgrims created demand for food, clothing, accommodation, transport, ritual objects and other services. Priests, artisans, merchants and workers gradually settled near important temples. This process encouraged the growth of temple towns.

Sources and uses of temple wealth

Sources of wealthMajor uses
Royal land grantsInstitutional maintenance and religious activities
Merchant patronageConstruction and cultural patronage
Pilgrim donationsWorship, festivals and charitable services
Assigned revenue rightsMaintenance and economic activities

In certain historical settings, wealthy temples also participated in lending, banking and commercial finance. Some rulers granted temples the right to receive specified taxes or dues. However, not every temple possessed these privileges.

Important historical examples

Thanjavur

Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu was an important Chola capital and temple town. The Rajarajeshvara Temple, also known as the Brihadisvara Temple, was built by Rajaraja Chola I.

The town contained markets, weaving communities, metalworkers and other occupational groups. Temple ceremonies and festivals generated demand for textiles, metal objects and specialised services.

Somnath

Somnath developed as an important religious and economic centre on the Gujarat coast. The movement of pilgrims and the provision of religious and commercial services illustrate the connection between sacred institutions and urban growth.

Ajmer and Pushkar

Ajmer developed around political, commercial and religious functions. The dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti became a major pilgrimage destination. Nearby Pushkar developed around its sacred lake and Hindu pilgrimage traditions.

The presence of these destinations in the same region demonstrates that different religious networks can coexist and contribute to a shared regional economy.

Trade routes and pilgrimage routes

Merchants and pilgrims frequently travelled along the same routes. Commercial settlements supplied food, accommodation, transport and protection. Religious establishments could provide resting places, learning centres and hospitality.

Buddhist monasteries located near passes through the Western Ghats benefited from their proximity to trade routes connecting western coastal ports with settlements in the Deccan.

Surat as the gateway to Mecca

During the Mughal period, Surat was a major centre of maritime trade with West Asia. It was also known as the Gate to Mecca because numerous pilgrim ships departed from its port.

Surat consequently illustrates how a commercial port could simultaneously support international pilgrimage, cultural exchange and the movement of religious travellers.

A temple town is not necessarily exclusively religious. Religious, administrative, commercial and artisanal functions may exist together in the same settlement.

Prelims focus

  • Temple towns grew through religious patronage, pilgrimage and related economic activity.
  • Thanjavur was both a Chola capital and a temple town.
  • Rajarajeshvara Temple was built by Rajaraja Chola I.
  • Some medieval temples participated in banking and commercial finance.
  • Surat was known as the Gate to Mecca.
  • Ajmer and Pushkar illustrate the coexistence of distinct pilgrimage traditions.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts – II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 6, pp. 75–80 and 84–85; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts – I, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 10, pp. 104–106.]
